content.title: Why Rick Pitino targeted ‘culture guys’ to build this year’s St. John’s roster
content.text: In each of his three seasons at St. John’s, head coach Rick Pitino has overseen a largely different roster. That’s the nature of the NIL and transfer-portal era. Player mobility is at an all-time high. While St. John’s delivered a similar level of success the past two years — winning the Big East’s regular-season and conference-tournament championships in both — Pitino said he assembled the 2025-26 roster with a different approach. “Last year, we had a terrific team. We knew all the players,” Pitino said ahead of the NCAA Tournament. “This year, we just went after culture guys — guys that we felt were really going to play for the name on the front, not worried about stats or making it somewhere else. Just totally bought in.” Among the experienced difference-makers that St. John’s added through the transfer portal last offseason were Bryce Hopkins, Dillon Mitchell, Oziyah Sellers, Dylan Darling, Ian Jackson and Joson Sanon. That core complemented star forward/center Zuby Ejiofor, who was the only starter to return. “Every single guy, we did our homework [on] and beyond that, and we got great culture guys,” Pitino said. “And it’s paid off very well for us.” Pitino often speaks about the challenge of building a culture and a cohesive roster when a program is turning over seven or eight players each season. The lack of familiarity contributed to the Red Storm’s slow start, as they began the season 9-5 before rattling off 20 wins in 21 games entering Sunday’s NCAA Tournament second-round meeting with Kansas in San Diego. But the strategy has worked for Pitino, 73, who led St. John’s to back-to-back NCAA Tournament appearances for the first time since 1998-2000, when the Johnnies went to three straight Big Dances. “Every program’s different. Arizona’s different than Duke. Duke and Arkansas are in the same boat. They’re going to get the top seven high-school players in the nation,” Pitino said. “We don’t build through the high-school ranks; we build through the portal. And we keep the guys that want to come back, and the ones that want to leave should leave.” Ejiofor spent his freshman season at Kansas before transferring to St. John’s, where he’s stood out as the rare modern player to play three seasons for the same school. Hopkins is at his third school, having previously played for Kentucky and Providence. So is Mitchell, who played for Texas and Cincinnati. “Even now, seeing him every day, I’m like, ‘I’m really playing for Coach Pitino.’ It really is kind of crazy,” Mitchell said. “Even when I first committed, my mom and everybody like that, they didn’t know too much about Coach P. When I came on my visit, I was starstruck, like I was meeting a celebrity. … Being with him every day and learning under him, it’s the best experience I’ve ever had.” St. John’s is set to look much different again next season, as Ejiofor, Mitchell, Hopkins and Sellers are all in their final year of NCAA eligibility. But Pitino should be able to find ready-made contributors through the portal again this offseason. Over the past three years, he’s proven to be quite capable of that, making the most of a format in which some college players stay longer to earn more NIL money and some international players come to the NCAA to get paid. “I look at the portal in a different way to most people, because I’ve been around so long,” Pitino said. “College basketball in the last two years, maybe three years, is the best product on the floor that I’ve seen in my lifetime.”
